summary: Derm Foundation is a machine learning model designed to accelerate AI development for skin image analysis for dermatology applications using pre-trained embeddings. It produces a 6144-dimensional embedding vector as output.
keywords: machine learning; dermatology; image analysis; embeddings; skin conditions
intended_use_and_workflow: Derm Foundation can reduce the training data, compute, and technical expertise necessary to develop task-specific models for skin image analysis. Embeddings can be used for classifying clinical conditions, scoring severity, identifying the body part, and determining image quality.
primary_intended_users: Businesses and institutions in healthcare and life sciences, researchers.
necessary_knowledge_expertise: Technical expertise to develop task-specific models for skin image analysis.
how_to_use: Use example code snippets, run the model locally, or create a production version using Model Garden. Use the API to retrieve embeddings from dermatology images stored in Google Cloud.
targeted_patient_population: Populations relevant to the datasets used in training, including teledermatology datasets from the United States and Colombia, a skin cancer dataset from Australia, and additional public images.
developer_supplied_warnings: The quality of Derm Foundation can degrade in extreme lighting or noise conditions. It was trained on data from a limited set of countries and settings and may not generalize well to other countries, patient populations, or image types.
model_limitations: Derm Foundation's quality can degrade in extreme lighting conditions. The base model was trained using potentially noisy or low-quality image-text pairs from the web. The fine-tuned model may not generalize well to data from other countries, patient populations, or image types not used in training. The model does not generate predictions or diagnoses on its own.
skin_type_representation_and_equity: Developers should validate any downstream application to understand performance using data that is appropriately representative of the intended use setting (e.g., skin tone/type, age, sex, gender etc.). The SFT (supervised fine-tuned) model was trained data from a limited set of countries (United States, Colombia, Australia, public images) and settings (mostly clinical).
outcomes_and_output: The model produces a 6144-dimensional embedding vector as output, which can be used for downstream tasks like classifying skin conditions and scoring severity.
type_and_value_of_solution_output: Embedding vector of floating point values (Dimensions: 6144)
explanation_for_how_an_output_is_generat: Derm Foundation is pre-trained on large amounts of labeled skin images to produce 6144 dimensional embeddings that capture dense features relevant for analyzing these images.
input_data_source: A large number of health-related image-text pairs from the public web and tele-dermatology datasets from the United States and Colombia, a skin cancer dataset from Australia, and additional public images.
output_input_data_type: Input: PNG image file 448 x 448 pixels
development_data_characterization: The images come from a mix of device types, including images from smartphone cameras, other cameras, and dermatoscopes. The images also have a mix of image takers; images may have been taken by clinicians during consultations or self-captured by patients.
training_data: Derm Foundation was trained in two stages: pre-training on image-text pairs from the internet and fine-tuning for condition classification using clinical datasets.
demographic_representativeness: The SFT (supervised fine-tuned) model was trained using data from the United States, Colombia, Australia, and public images. The images come from a mix of device types and image takers [SOURCE 1]. Developers should validate downstream applications to understand performance using data that is representative of the intended use setting [SOURCE 1].
dataset_transparency: The Derm Foundation model was trained on a large number of public image-text pairs from the internet [SOURCE 1]. It was also fine-tuned on clinical datasets from the United States, Colombia, Australia, and additional public images [SOURCE 1]. Labeling sources included image-caption pairs, dermatologist-provided condition labels, and clinical dataset labels [SOURCE 1].
skin_tone_diversity: As with any research, developers should ensure any downstream application is validated to understand performance using data that is appropriately representative of the intended use setting for the specific application (e.g., skin tone/type, age, sex, gender etc.) [SOURCE 1].
relevance_of_training_data_to_intended_p: The SFT (supervised fine-tuned) model was trained using data from a limited set of countries (United States, Colombia, Australia, public images) and settings (mostly clinical) [SOURCE 1]. It may not generalize well to data from other countries, patient populations, or image types not used in training [SOURCE 1].
usefulness_efficacy_goal_of_metrics: Derm Foundation was evaluated for data-efficient accuracy across a range of skin-related classifications tasks [SOURCE 1]. The goal is to reduce training data, compute, and expertise for skin image analysis [SOURCE 1].
usefulness_efficacy_result: Training a linear classifier on Derm-Foundations embeddings were substantially more performant (10-15% increase in accuracy) than doing the same for a standard BiT-M model across different proportions of training data [SOURCE 1]. Models built on top of the Derm Foundation embeddings achieved higher quality compared to standard pre-trained image models [SOURCE 6].
usefulness_efficacy_interpretation: The results demonstrate that the Derm Foundation tool can serve as a useful starting point to accelerate skin-related modeling tasks [SOURCE 4].
usefulness_efficacy_test_type: Linear classifier on frozen embeddings were used to evaluate the model [SOURCE 4].
usefulness_efficacy_testing_data_descrip: The model was trained and evaluated using tele-dermatology datasets from the United States and Colombia, a skin cancer dataset from Australia, and additional public images [SOURCE 1].
usefulness_efficacy_validation_process_a: Model training involved varying dataset sizes (12.5%, 25%, 50%, 100%) to compare embedding-based linear classifiers against fine-tuning [SOURCE 4].
